meta.description: Composable UX & AI research methods. Each block is tagged for filtering by practical constraints: phase, budget, participants, effort, question type. Merge of Cambridge HCI for AI Systems (2024) and Rohrer's UX research methods framework.

phase.strategize: Finding direction, understanding the problem space

answers.how_to_fix: What's broken and how to improve it

qual_quant.qualitative: Direct observation or open-ended — why and how to fix
qual_quant.quantitative: Measured via instrument — how many and how much
qual_quant.both: Can produce either depending on protocol

attitudinal_behavioral.attitudinal: What people say, believe, or prefer

context.natural: Observing real use with minimal interference
context.scripted: Controlled tasks to focus on specific flows
context.limited: Abstracted or partial version of the product
context.decontextualized: No product use during the study
context.analytical: No users involved — expert or computational analysis

dimensions.effort: low | medium | high — setup, execution, and analysis combined
dimensions.budget: low | medium | high — direct costs including participant compensation
dimensions.duration: hours | days | weeks — wall-clock time from start to findings
dimensions.expertise: low | medium | high — specialist skill needed to run it well

methods.name: Solution-Neutral Problem Statement
methods.description: Abstract the design brief 3–6 levels up to strip out solution fixation. Forces the team to define what problem they're actually solving before jumping to features.
methods.when: First step, before any design or prototyping. Essential when the brief already contains an implied solution.
methods.watch_out: Can feel too abstract if the team isn't used to it — anchor with concrete examples.

methods.name: System Boundary Definition
methods.description: Delineate what is inside the design scope vs. external context. Draws a line around what you're responsible for designing and what you treat as given.
methods.when: Immediately after problem framing, before functional modelling.
methods.watch_out: Too narrow a boundary hides integration risks; too wide makes design intractable.

methods.name: Requirements Specification
methods.description: Living document encoding user, technical, business, and regulatory constraints. Each requirement should be testable and traceable to a source.
methods.when: Initialized early, updated continuously through design and the product's lifetime.
methods.watch_out: Becomes shelfware if not actively maintained. Assign ownership.

methods.name: Sampling Frame
methods.description: Profile target audience via behavioural, technological, and demographic criteria. Defines who you recruit and ensures your research covers the right population segments.
methods.when: Before any user research. Used for recruitment screening and persona definition.
methods.watch_out: A bad frame biases every downstream study. Validate assumptions about your audience early.

methods.name: Personas
methods.description: Fictional characters representing user groups, grounded in research data. Encode goals, frustrations, context of use, and technical fluency.
methods.when: During requirements elicitation and throughout design evaluation. Keep them alive, not filed away.
methods.watch_out: Personas without research backing become fiction that confirms biases.

methods.name: Traceability Analysis
methods.description: Track requirement sources and interdependencies to manage change. When one requirement shifts, you can see which others are affected.
methods.when: Whenever requirements shift — to assess cascade effects on other specs.
methods.watch_out: Only useful if requirements are actually structured and numbered.

methods.name: Interviews (Non-Directed)
methods.description: Structured or semi-structured 1:1 interviews with six phases: intro, warm-up, general, deep focus, retrospective, wrap-up. The core generative research method for understanding motivations, mental models, and unmet needs.
methods.when: Early generative stages when deep qualitative insight into motivations is needed. Also useful mid-design for evaluating concepts.
methods.watch_out: People are bad at predicting their own future behavior. Triangulate with behavioral methods.

methods.name: Focus Groups
methods.description: Moderated group discussions (6–10 people) for surfacing preferences, priorities, and reactions. Good for idea generation and seeing how opinions form socially.
methods.when: Early, for feature prioritization and idea generation. Not for predicting actual behavior or usability.
methods.watch_out: Groupthink and dominant voices distort results. Never use alone for design decisions.

methods.name: Field Visits / Ethnographic Studies
methods.description: Observing users in their natural environment — workplace, home, or wherever they actually use the product. Reveals the gap between what people say and what they do.
methods.when: When there's a gap between reported and actual behavior. Essential for understanding real context of use.
methods.watch_out: Expensive and time-consuming. Observer effect is real — people behave differently when watched.

methods.name: Diary Studies
methods.description: Users log activities, frustrations, and learnings at regular intervals over days or weeks. Captures longitudinal patterns without the researcher being present.
methods.when: When you need longitudinal data about habits, pain points, or context changes over time.
methods.watch_out: Participant dropout is high. Keep entries short and provide reminders.

methods.name: Experience Sampling Method (ESM)
methods.description: Mobile prompts with short tasks or surveys at random or triggered moments throughout the day. Captures in-the-moment experience without recall bias.
methods.when: When you need self-reports at the moment of experience rather than retrospective accounts.
methods.watch_out: Too many prompts cause fatigue and dropout. Keep surveys under 30 seconds.

methods.name: Surveys
methods.description: Closed and open-ended questions for statistical generalization. Scalable way to measure attitudes, satisfaction, and demographics across a population.
methods.when: Profiling, satisfaction tracking, feature prioritization. Must be validated with behavioral methods for anything beyond stated preferences.
methods.watch_out: Survey design is harder than it looks. Leading questions, double-barrels, and response bias are common.

methods.name: Participatory Design
methods.description: Users actively co-design by arranging, modifying, or creating design elements. They become collaborators rather than subjects.
methods.when: When domain expertise lives with users and you need their input on structure, not just feedback.
methods.watch_out: Designs reflect what users can imagine, not necessarily what they need. Don't take outputs as specs.

methods.name: Card Sorting
methods.description: Users organize topics into groups that make sense to them. Reveals mental models for information architecture. Open sort (users create categories) or closed sort (categories given).
methods.when: Designing navigation, menus, or content structure. When you need to understand how users categorize.
methods.watch_out: Only tests mental models in isolation — doesn't tell you if users can find things in a real interface.

methods.name: Tree Testing
methods.description: Users navigate a text-only hierarchy to find items. Tests whether your information architecture works without visual design as a confound.
methods.when: After card sorting or IA redesign, to validate the hierarchy before building the UI.
methods.watch_out: Strips all context — real navigation uses visual cues, breadcrumbs, search.

methods.name: Concept Testing
methods.description: Present an expression of a product idea — sketch, storyboard, landing page, video — to see if users understand the value proposition and would want it.
methods.when: Before committing to building. Tests desirability and comprehension of the core idea.
methods.watch_out: Positive reactions to concepts don't predict actual adoption. People are polite.

methods.name: Desirability Studies
methods.description: Users select words from a curated list (e.g., Microsoft's Product Reaction Cards) to describe their reaction to a design. Quantifies emotional and aesthetic response.
methods.when: When choosing between visual directions or measuring brand perception of a design.
methods.watch_out: Word lists constrain response. Supplement with open-ended follow-up.

methods.name: Function Structures
methods.description: Model the system as functions connected via flows of signals, energy, and material. Makes subfunction interactions explicit through inputs and outputs.
methods.when: During conceptual design, to decompose the system and understand what each part does before choosing solutions.
methods.watch_out: Can become overly abstract. Ground each function in observable user or system behavior.

methods.name: FAST Diagrams
methods.description: Decompose abstract functions into concrete, time-ordered verb-noun functions. Reads left-to-right (why → how) and traces workflows to ensure nothing is missed.
methods.when: After function structures, to ensure no subfunction is overlooked in the workflow.
methods.watch_out: Requires discipline in the verb-noun format. Vague functions signal incomplete understanding.

methods.name: Morphological Charts
methods.description: Table mapping each function to candidate function carriers (solutions). Each row is a function; each column is a possible way to achieve it. Combine across rows to generate concepts.
methods.when: After function modelling, to generate combinatorial design concepts systematically.
methods.watch_out: Combinatorial explosion. Not every combination is viable — use engineering judgment to prune.

methods.name: Concept Evaluation (Weighted Scoring)
methods.description: Score concepts against weighted criteria. Supplement with narrative rationale — the score is a conversation starter, not a decision maker.
methods.when: After generating concepts, to narrow the field. Always pair the numbers with qualitative judgment.
methods.watch_out: Over-trusting the score kills good ideas. The matrix is a discussion tool, not a verdict.

methods.name: Explicit Trade-off Logging
methods.description: Document design dimensions, options considered, decisions made, and risks explicitly ignored. Prevents implicit decisions that cause latent failures.
methods.when: At every design decision point. If someone asks 'why did we do it this way?' the log should have the answer.
methods.watch_out: Only valuable if maintained. A log nobody updates is worse than no log.

methods.name: Controllable vs. Uncontrollable Parameter Analysis
methods.description: Classify parameters into those the designer can tune (font size, threshold, delay) vs. environmental or user-intrinsic factors (lighting, expertise, age). Design for the controllable; test sensitivity to the uncontrollable.
methods.when: After function modelling, to identify what you can optimize vs. what you need to be robust against.
methods.watch_out: Uncontrollable parameters are often the ones that matter most. Don't ignore them just because you can't tune them.

methods.name: Wizard of Oz
methods.description: A human secretly simulates AI or system behavior while users interact with the interface as if it were real. Tests the interaction concept before the technology exists.
methods.when: When the AI is unavailable, too expensive, or too risky to build without validating the interaction first.
methods.watch_out: The wizard's performance sets user expectations. If the wizard is better than the eventual AI, you've validated the wrong thing.

methods.name: KLM-GOMS
methods.description: Predict expert task completion times using keystroke-level operators (K, P, B, BB, H, M, W). Compare interface efficiencies on paper without recruiting anyone.
methods.when: Very early design, to compare layout or workflow alternatives on raw efficiency before prototyping.
methods.watch_out: Only models expert, error-free performance. Says nothing about learnability or error recovery.

methods.name: Computational Experiments (Oracle Simulation)
methods.description: Simulate ideal or imperfect users computationally to explore parameter configurations. Test sensitivity to noise, latency, or accuracy before involving real people.
methods.when: Early design — optimize UI parameters or test how robust the system is to imperfect input before heavy prototyping.
methods.watch_out: Simulated users are only as good as your model of user behavior. Validate assumptions.

methods.name: Function Allocation Strategies
methods.description: Decide what the human does vs. what the system does. Three strategies: maximize automation, allocate to most capable agent, or maximize economic efficiency.
methods.when: After functional modelling, before selecting automation types. The foundational decision in human-AI system design.
methods.watch_out: Leftover allocation (give humans what the machine can't do) creates worst-case human roles. Design the human role intentionally.

methods.name: Types of Automation
methods.description: Classify automation by cognitive stage: Acquisition (sensing), Analysis (processing), Decision (choosing), Action (executing), Adaptive (learning). Maps to human information processing.
methods.when: When diagnosing which cognitive stage each function targets — helps decide what kind of AI support to build.
methods.watch_out: Real systems often span multiple types. Don't force a single label.

methods.name: Levels of Automation (1–10)
methods.description: Scale from no assistance (1) through decision support (5) to full autonomous control (10). Sets the human's involvement level for each function.
methods.when: After identifying automation candidates, to decide how much human involvement each function needs.
methods.watch_out: Higher levels aren't always better. Level 6 (human can veto) requires the human to actually monitor, which they often won't.

methods.name: Types & Levels of Automation Framework (7-step)
methods.description: Iterative framework combining types and levels with evaluation criteria. Loop: allocate functions → set automation level → evaluate against human-centered criteria → redesign.
methods.when: During automation design when you need a structured process, not just gut feeling about what to automate.
methods.watch_out: The framework is iterative — doing one pass defeats the purpose.

methods.name: TPR / FPR / ROC Analysis
methods.description: Assess classifier performance via true/false positive rates and ROC curves. Shows the tradeoff between catching real positives and generating false alarms.
methods.when: Evaluating automation reliability for any classification task. Critical for alert systems, content moderation, medical screening.
methods.watch_out: ROC curves hide the base rate problem. A 99% accurate test is useless if the condition has 0.01% prevalence.

methods.name: Risk = Likelihood × Impact
methods.description: Quantitative estimation of risk severity. Simple formula that forces explicit thinking about both how likely a failure is and how bad it would be.
methods.when: During automation evaluation to set acceptable thresholds. When deciding what error rates are tolerable.
methods.watch_out: Garbage in, garbage out. If your likelihood estimate is a guess, the product is a guess too.

methods.name: Direct Manipulation
methods.description: Design principle: interaction via visible objects, physical actions, and immediate incremental reversible feedback. Maximizes user sense of control and agency.
methods.when: GUI design as a baseline principle. Tension with AI systems that act autonomously.
methods.watch_out: Not everything can be directly manipulated. AI outputs often need indirect interaction patterns.

methods.name: Gulf of Execution / Gulf of Evaluation
methods.description: Cognitive distance between user goals and system state. Gulf of execution: can the user figure out how to act? Gulf of evaluation: can they tell what happened?
methods.when: During interaction review — diagnostic tool for why users struggle with an interface.
methods.watch_out: Descriptive, not prescriptive. Identifies the gap but doesn't tell you how to close it.

methods.name: Seven Stages of Action (Norman)
methods.description: Perceive → Interpret → Evaluate → Formulate goals → Form intentions → Specify actions → Execute. Diagnostic model for mapping where exactly an interaction breaks down.
methods.when: When you've found a usability problem and need to pinpoint which cognitive step is failing.
methods.watch_out: Works best for discrete tasks. Less useful for open-ended or exploratory interaction.

methods.name: Mixed-Initiative Interfaces (Horvitz)
methods.description: Couple direct manipulation with automated services. Either the user or the AI can take initiative depending on confidence, urgency, and cost of interruption.
methods.when: When AI assistance is needed but interruption cost and uncertainty must be balanced. The core pattern for AI copilots.
methods.watch_out: Getting the threshold wrong either nags the user or hides useful suggestions.

methods.name: Programming by Example
methods.description: System induces programs from user demonstrations. User shows a pattern; system generalizes it; user confirms before automation applies. Control stays with the user.
methods.when: For repetitive tasks where the user can demonstrate the pattern and wants to retain control over automation.
methods.watch_out: Edge cases in generalization. Users rarely demonstrate the full range of variation.

methods.name: Prompt-Based Interaction
methods.description: Natural language or keyword prompts triggering generative output. The dominant interaction pattern for LLMs. Analogous to command entry — powerful but has discoverability problems.
methods.when: LLM-based systems. Requires discoverability safeguards because users can't see what's possible.
methods.watch_out: The blank prompt box is the modern equivalent of the command line. Most users won't know what to type.

methods.name: H-Metaphor / Shared Control
methods.description: Horse-rider model: loose rein (system handles low-level control) vs. tight rein (user micromanages). Framework for thinking about shared control granularity.
methods.when: Designing shared control in vehicles, robotics, assistive tech, or any system where user and AI share a continuous control loop.
methods.watch_out: Metaphors aid thinking but can mislead. Horses have agency; AI does not.

methods.name: Four Levels of Shared Control
methods.description: Strategic (what), Tactical (how), Operational (moment-to-moment), Execution (motor). Framework for deciding what granularity of control to delegate.
methods.when: When designing joint human-AI systems and deciding which layer of control the human keeps.
methods.watch_out: Users often want strategic control but are forced into operational. Check the mismatch.

methods.name: Intentional Binding / Agency Measurement
methods.description: Perceived time compression between action and outcome. When people feel agency, they perceive their action and its effect as closer together in time.
methods.when: Experimental research — quantifying loss of agency from automation or mediated interfaces.
methods.watch_out: Lab-only method. Requires precise timing equipment and careful experimental design.

methods.name: Supervisory Control
methods.description: Human monitors AI via displays and intervenes when needed. The dominant pattern for high-automation domains — air traffic control, process monitoring, decision support.
methods.when: High-automation domains where the AI handles routine operation and the human handles exceptions.
methods.watch_out: Vigilance decrement is real — humans are terrible monitors. Design for re-engagement, not just surveillance.

methods.name: Human Computation
methods.description: Delegate steps too hard for AI to human workers at scale (reCAPTCHA, Mechanical Turk, content moderation). The AI handles what it can; humans fill the gaps.
methods.when: When AI cannot reliably solve a subtask but humans can — and you have enough volume to justify the pipeline.
methods.watch_out: Ethics of labor practices. The humans in the loop are real workers who need fair pay and healthy conditions.

methods.name: Interactive Machine Learning / Machine Teaching
methods.description: Users incrementally refine a model by correcting errors and labeling data. Requires four UI components: sample review, feedback assignment, model inspection, and task overview.
methods.when: When domain expertise must be injected post-deployment. The model learns from use, guided by the user.
methods.watch_out: Requires sustained user engagement. If users stop correcting, the model stops improving — or drifts.

methods.name: Dimensionality Reduction (PCA, t-SNE, Sammon)
methods.description: Project high-dimensional data to 2D/3D to reveal clusters, outliers, and structure. Essential for making model internals or feature spaces visually inspectable.
methods.when: Data exploration and model diagnostics. When you need to understand what the feature space looks like.
methods.watch_out: 2D projections lie. Distances in t-SNE are not meaningful across clusters.

methods.name: Feature Selection / Feature Engineering
methods.description: Hand-pick or compute the most informative dimensions using domain knowledge. Decides what the model should pay attention to.
methods.when: When domain knowledge exists to guide model attention. Also useful for reducing model complexity and increasing interpretability.
methods.watch_out: Feature selection bakes in assumptions about what matters. Those assumptions can be wrong.

methods.name: Uncertainty Visualization
methods.description: Error bars, box-and-whisker plots, fan charts for predictions over time. Makes model confidence visible rather than hidden behind a single point estimate.
methods.when: Whenever presenting model outputs with inherent uncertainty. Especially important for forecasts and recommendations.
methods.watch_out: Users often ignore uncertainty info or misinterpret it. Test comprehension, don't assume it.

methods.name: Confidence Score Calibration
methods.description: Present posterior probabilities over alternatives rather than just the top pick. Lets users see how confident the model actually is.
methods.when: When users must choose among AI-generated options. Requires that users understand what the scores mean.
methods.watch_out: Uncalibrated confidence scores are worse than none. A model that says 90% but is right 60% of the time breeds over-trust.

methods.name: LIME
methods.description: Fit a simple local interpretable model around a single prediction to explain it. Model-agnostic — works on any classifier by perturbing inputs and observing output changes.
methods.when: When end users or auditors need to understand why a specific prediction was made.
methods.watch_out: Local explanations can be misleading if the locality is wrong. And the simple model might not capture the real decision boundary.

methods.name: Anchors
methods.description: Generate simple IF-THEN rules that are robust in a restricted region of feature space. High-precision explanations for specific decision boundaries.
methods.when: When you need rule-based explanations that hold reliably in a neighborhood, not just for a single point.
methods.watch_out: Rules can be brittle at the boundary edges. Users may overgeneralize them.

methods.name: Saliency / Feature Highlighting
methods.description: Visually indicate which input features drove a classification — heatmaps, attention overlays, highlighted regions. Most intuitive for image or text inputs.
methods.when: Computer vision and perceptual domains. When showing 'what the model looked at' helps build appropriate trust.
methods.watch_out: Dominant features may be spurious. A model highlighting grass in a 'cow' classification is using a shortcut, not understanding.

methods.name: Doshi-Velez & Kim Evaluation Framework
methods.description: Three levels for evaluating interpretability methods: Application-oriented (does it help on the real task?), Human-oriented (can users predict/simulate/counterfactual?), Functionally-oriented (does the explanation method have good formal properties?).
methods.when: Deciding how to evaluate an interpretability method before deployment. Picks the right rigor level.
methods.watch_out: Application-oriented is the gold standard but most expensive. Don't skip it for safety-critical systems.

methods.name: Mistake vs. Slip Analysis
methods.description: Distinguish errors of intention (wrong plan) from errors of execution (right plan, wrong action). Determines whether the fix is training, UI redesign, or procedural change.
methods.when: Human error diagnosis — when users make errors and you need to know why before redesigning.
methods.watch_out: Requires observing or reconstructing the error context. Post-hoc reports are unreliable.

methods.name: SRK Framework (Skill-Rule-Knowledge)
methods.description: Classify behavior as Skill-based (automatic), Rule-based (if-then), or Knowledge-based (novel reasoning). Diagnoses at which cognitive level an error occurred.
methods.when: After identifying an error, to target redesign at the right level: perception (skill), procedures (rule), or training/information (knowledge).
methods.watch_out: Real behavior often mixes levels. A novice doing knowledge-based work eventually automates to skill.

methods.name: System Mapping (6 diagram types)
methods.description: Task, Information, Organisational, System, Process, and Communication diagrams. Maps the full system context before doing risk assessment.
methods.when: Before risk assessment — to understand the system boundary, actors, data flows, and decision points.
methods.watch_out: Maps are not the territory. Update them when the system changes.

methods.name: Hazard Identification
methods.description: Identify sources with potential to cause adverse effects — technical failures, user errors, environmental conditions, adversarial inputs.
methods.when: First step of risk management. Before you can assess risk, you need to know what can go wrong.
methods.watch_out: You can't assess risks you haven't identified. Invest in creative what-if thinking.

methods.name: Exposure Analysis
methods.description: Determine whether a hazard actually reaches users or systems. A hazard that exists but never contacts anyone isn't a risk.
methods.when: After hazard identification — to filter hazards into actual risks worth mitigating.
methods.watch_out: Exposure can change. A hazard that's unexposed today might be exposed after a feature change.

methods.name: Risk Management Cycle (5 steps)
methods.description: Hazard identification → Estimation → Evaluation → Control → Monitoring. Continuous, not one-shot — risks change as the system evolves.
methods.when: Throughout design, deployment, and operation. Revisit after any significant change.
methods.watch_out: Monitoring is the step everyone skips. Schedule it or it won't happen.

methods.name: SWIFT (Structured What-If Technique)
methods.description: Team-based scenario analysis using a prompt vocabulary ('what if the user...', 'what if the model...'). Fast, creative, and good at surfacing novel risks.
methods.when: Early risk identification workshops. When you need to explore scenarios that formal methods might miss.
methods.watch_out: Quality depends entirely on the team's imagination and domain knowledge.

methods.name: FMEA (Failure Mode & Effects Analysis)
methods.description: Component-by-component failure mode analysis scoring probability, severity, and detectability. Produces a Risk Priority Number (RPN) for each failure mode.
methods.when: Systematic, quantitative risk assessment at the component level. Good for complex systems with many parts.
methods.watch_out: RPN multiplication can be misleading — a 2×5 and a 5×2 have the same score but very different implications.

methods.name: Fault Trees
methods.description: Top-down tree of logical AND/OR relationships leading to a fault event. Traces how combinations of failures or conditions produce the top-level hazard.
methods.when: Root-cause analysis and tracing interdependencies between failures. When you need to understand causal chains.
methods.watch_out: Trees assume you know all the branches. Unknown failure modes won't appear.

methods.name: Risk Matrix
methods.description: 2D likelihood vs. impact plot for prioritization and communication. Colors code risk severity. Simple enough for stakeholder conversations.
methods.when: After SWIFT/FMEA — to communicate and rank risks for decision makers who won't read a full FMEA table.
methods.watch_out: Oversimplifies by design. Don't mistake the matrix for the analysis.

methods.name: Fjeld et al. Governance Principles
methods.description: Eight principles: Privacy, Accountability, Safety & Security, Transparency & Explainability, Fairness & Non-discrimination, Human Control, Professional Responsibility, Promotion of Human Values.
methods.when: Policy and design review checkpoints. When defining governance structure for AI systems.
methods.watch_out: Principles without operationalization are performative. Each needs measurable criteria.

methods.name: Alignment & Specification Review
methods.description: Check for specification gaming, loopholes, reward hacking, and emergent misalignment. Does the system do what you meant, or what you literally specified?
methods.when: When deploying adaptive or learning systems. Required for safety-critical AI.
methods.watch_out: Alignment is not a one-time check. Systems that learn can drift after passing review.

methods.name: Verification (Build the thing right)
methods.description: Confirm all requirements are met. Maps each requirement to a verification method (Inspection, Demonstration, Test, Analysis) via the VCRM.
methods.when: After implementation, before validation. Checks conformance to spec.
methods.watch_out: Passing verification doesn't mean the product is useful — just that it matches the spec.

methods.name: Validation (Build the right thing)
methods.description: Confirm the system is fit for purpose. Goes beyond spec compliance to ask: does this actually solve the user's problem?
methods.when: After verification. Via pre-deployment pilot or post-deployment study with real users.
methods.watch_out: Validation with unrepresentative users validates nothing. Use your sampling frame.

methods.name: Heuristic Evaluation (Nielsen)
methods.description: Experts inspect the UI against established heuristics, reporting frequency, severity, and persistence of violations. Fast, cheap, and catches the obvious problems.
methods.when: Early validation — before user testing. When budget or time is tight. Best with 3–5 evaluators.
methods.watch_out: Finds surface-level issues, misses deep workflow problems. Evaluators are not users.

methods.name: Amershi et al. Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction
methods.description: 18 heuristics organized by phase: initially (set expectations), during interaction (support efficient correction), when wrong (support recovery), over time (encourage granular feedback). The AI-specific equivalent of Nielsen's heuristics.
methods.when: Evaluating AI-infused interfaces specifically. Use alongside traditional heuristics, not instead of them.
methods.watch_out: Guidelines are necessary but not sufficient. They catch violations but not novel interaction problems.

methods.name: Usability Testing (Lab / Remote)
methods.description: Users attempt tasks while researchers observe. Moderated (researcher guides, probes, adjusts) or unmoderated (remote, large-scale, automated). The backbone of formative evaluation.
methods.when: Formative: during design to find and fix problems. Summative: after launch to benchmark. Most versatile method.
methods.watch_out: Lab setting is artificial. Tasks may not represent real use. Moderated tests don't scale.

methods.name: Usability Benchmarking
methods.description: Tightly scripted study measuring task success, time, errors, and satisfaction across participants. Produces reliable metrics for comparison over time or against competitors.
methods.when: Summative: measuring product performance against earlier versions or competitors. Requires consistent protocol.
methods.watch_out: Expensive to run well. Metrics without context are dangerous — a fast wrong answer isn't a good outcome.

methods.name: Unmoderated Remote UX Testing
methods.description: Participants complete tasks independently via a testing platform. Scales to large samples, captures real-environment behavior, but loses the ability to probe.
methods.when: When you need larger samples than moderated testing allows, or when geographic reach matters.
methods.watch_out: No moderator means no follow-up questions. You see what happened but not always why.

methods.name: Centaur Evaluations
methods.description: Humans and AI cooperate to solve a task together, measuring the combined performance. Tests the human-AI team, not the model in isolation.
methods.when: When isolated model benchmarks don't capture real-world performance because the system is designed for human-AI collaboration.
methods.watch_out: Results depend heavily on the human's skill and strategy. Report both individual and team performance.

methods.name: Dynamic Benchmarks
methods.description: Introduce human involvement into benchmarking to better mirror real-world interaction. Addresses dataset leakage and static benchmark staleness.
methods.when: When static benchmarks have leaked into training data or don't represent real use anymore.
methods.watch_out: Designing good dynamic benchmarks is itself a research problem.

methods.name: Between-Subjects Experiment
methods.description: Each participant sees one condition. Avoids learning/carryover effects but requires more participants to achieve statistical power.
methods.when: When learning effects are asymmetrical, conditions can't be counterbalanced, or the study involves deception.
methods.watch_out: Individual differences are confounded with conditions unless you randomize properly.

methods.name: Within-Subjects Experiment + Counterbalancing
methods.description: Each participant sees all conditions with order rotated to cancel learning effects. Default for comparing interfaces — controls individual variability and needs fewer participants.
methods.when: Default for interface comparison. Only avoid if learning effects are asymmetrical.
methods.watch_out: Counterbalancing doesn't eliminate learning — it distributes it. Check for asymmetric transfer.

methods.name: Asymmetrical Skill-Transfer Check
methods.description: Test whether one experimental condition teaches users more than the other, which would break counterbalancing assumptions.
methods.when: When pilot data suggests learning effects are not symmetrical. Determines whether within-subjects is viable.
methods.watch_out: Small pilot samples may not reveal the asymmetry. When in doubt, go between-subjects.

methods.name: Threats to Validity Checklist
methods.description: Systematic check for Internal (confounds), External (generalizability), and Construct (metric alignment) threats. Review before running any user study.
methods.when: During experimental design review — before investing in data collection.
methods.watch_out: Knowing the threats doesn't mean you can eliminate all of them. Document what you can't control.

methods.name: Hypothesis Testing (Frequentist / Bayesian)
methods.description: Infer systematic effects vs. noise. Frequentist: p-value thresholding, power analysis. Bayesian: posterior probability updating, credible intervals.
methods.when: After data collection — the statistical backbone of any controlled study.
methods.watch_out: p < 0.05 is not a magic number. Report effect sizes, confidence intervals, and practical significance.

methods.name: Appropriation Analysis (Dix)
methods.description: Study how users adopt, adapt, personalize, tailor, and socially spread a system. Reveals shadow practices — the real workflows users build around your product.
methods.when: Post-deployment. Essential for understanding what users actually do vs. what you designed for.
methods.watch_out: Appropriation can be positive (users find creative uses) or negative (workarounds for broken features). Don't romanticize it.

methods.name: Deployment Study Methods
methods.description: Post-launch research toolkit: logging, surveys, review mining, field observation, A/B testing. Continuous improvement and detecting emergent misuse or value.
methods.when: Post-launch, continuously. The product is live — now you learn from real use.
methods.watch_out: Logging without analysis is data hoarding. Decide what you're looking for before you instrument.

methods.name: A/B Testing
methods.description: Present design variations to random samples of real users while holding all else constant. Measures the causal effect of specific design changes on behavior.
methods.when: When you have enough traffic to reach statistical significance and a clear metric to optimize.
methods.watch_out: Optimizing for clicks can degrade the overall experience. Choose metrics that reflect real value.

methods.name: Clickstream / Analytics
methods.description: Analyze actual usage data — page views, click paths, funnels, feature adoption, error rates. The continuous behavioral signal from your live product.
methods.when: Post-launch, continuously. When you need to know what users actually do at scale.
methods.watch_out: Analytics show what but not why. A 40% drop-off tells you nothing about the reason.

methods.name: Eye Tracking
methods.description: Track where users look, in what order, and for how long. Reveals visual attention patterns, scan paths, and areas of confusion or neglect.
methods.when: When visual hierarchy and attention flow matter — landing pages, dashboards, complex forms, ad placement.
methods.watch_out: Looking at something doesn't mean understanding it. Fixation ≠ comprehension.

methods.name: Intercept Surveys
methods.description: Short surveys triggered during or after real product use — a pop-up after checkout, a satisfaction prompt after task completion. Captures attitudes in context.
methods.when: When you need attitudinal data tied to specific moments in real use, not recalled later.
methods.watch_out: Interrupting users to ask about their experience... interrupts their experience. Keep it very short.

methods.name: Friction Intensity Scale
methods.description: Calibrated intervention levels for AI responses: None → Citations → Progressive Disclosure → Fragility Markers → Triangulation + Gating. Higher stakes = more friction.
methods.when: Designing LLM response patterns where blind agreement is dangerous.
methods.watch_out: Too much friction kills utility. Too little enables harm. Calibrate per domain.

methods.name: Decision Paths
methods.description: Structured trade-off exploration for preference-dependent choices. Present multiple paths with explicit trade-offs rather than a single recommendation.
methods.when: When the right answer depends on the user's values or constraints, not on facts alone.
methods.watch_out: Don't present decision paths for single-answer factual queries — it looks like hedging.

methods.name: Progressive Disclosure
methods.description: Layered revelation of detail. Show the essential answer first; let users drill into evidence, caveats, and methodology on demand.
methods.when: Medium-stakes factual or research queries. Not for casual time-critical questions.
methods.watch_out: If the critical caveat is hidden behind a disclosure, users who need it most may never see it.

methods.name: Grounded Citations
methods.description: Attach verifiable sources to claims. Not decorative bibliography — citations that the user can actually check.
methods.when: Verifiable claims and current events. Avoid for pure reasoning or creative tasks where 'source' doesn't apply.
methods.watch_out: Fake citations are worse than no citations. Only cite what you can actually verify.

methods.name: Fragility Markers
methods.description: Label uncertainty and conditionality of answers. Make explicit what would need to be true for the advice to hold, and what could invalidate it.
methods.when: Conditional advice and personalized recommendations. Avoid for universal established facts.
methods.watch_out: Marking everything as fragile makes the markers meaningless. Reserve for genuinely conditional claims.

methods.name: Triangulation
methods.description: Require cross-referencing multiple sources or methods before confidence. The epistemological core of rigorous research — no single source is trusted alone.
methods.when: High-stakes domains (medical, legal, financial). When the cost of being wrong justifies the effort of checking.
methods.watch_out: Three wrong sources don't make a right answer. Triangulation requires independent sources.

methods.name: Role Buttons
methods.description: User-initiated pushback modes: devil's advocate, steelman, challenge. Lets the user control how much friction they want rather than imposing it.
methods.when: Any context where the user may want to stress-test a conclusion. User-controlled, not system-imposed.
methods.watch_out: Buttons nobody clicks are clutter. Test whether users actually use them.

methods.name: Domain Mapping by Stakes
methods.description: Assign friction pattern combinations per domain and question type. Medical gets triangulation + gating; casual chat gets citations at most.
methods.when: Configuring safety-critical LLM interfaces for specific professional domains.
methods.watch_out: Domain boundaries blur. A casual health question can become life-critical in one sentence.

methods.name: Contextual Inquiry
methods.description: Observe and interview users in their actual work environment while they perform real tasks. The researcher is an apprentice; the user is the expert. Unlike lab usability testing, you see the full context — interruptions, workarounds, tools taped to monitors, the things people never mention in interviews because they've stopped noticing.
methods.when: Early in a project when you don't yet understand the work domain. Essential when users' stated workflows differ from their actual behavior, or when the environment itself shapes how the tool is used.
methods.watch_out: Not the same as field visits — contextual inquiry has a specific master/apprentice structure with interpretation sessions. Without the structure it's just hanging around.

methods.name: Cognitive Walkthrough
methods.description: Step through a task action by action, asking at each step: will the user know what to do? Will they see the correct action? Will they understand the feedback? Unlike heuristic evaluation (which checks against a list), cognitive walkthrough simulates a first-time user's thought process and exposes learnability failures.
methods.when: Before usability testing, especially for onboarding flows, setup wizards, or any task where first-time success matters. Works on prototypes, live products, or even paper sketches.
methods.watch_out: Only tests one path per walkthrough. Doesn't catch errors of commission — only whether the correct action is discoverable. Pair with heuristic evaluation for full coverage.

methods.name: Think-Aloud Protocol
methods.description: Users verbalize their thoughts continuously while performing tasks. Concurrent think-aloud captures the reasoning in real time; retrospective think-aloud uses a recording as a prompt after the session. The most direct window into what users actually notice, expect, and misunderstand — not what they report afterward.
methods.when: During any usability evaluation where understanding the user's reasoning matters more than task-completion time. Can be layered onto usability testing, concept testing, or prototype evaluation.
methods.watch_out: Concurrent think-aloud changes behavior — users slow down and sometimes perform better because they're being more deliberate. Retrospective avoids this but introduces recall bias. Know which tradeoff you're making.

methods.name: Affinity Diagramming
methods.description: Take all the observations, quotes, and data points from research sessions and sort them bottom-up into clusters. No predefined categories — the structure emerges from the data. The physical version uses sticky notes on a wall; the digital version uses Miro or FigJam. The point is to find patterns you didn't expect, not to confirm the ones you did.
methods.when: After any qualitative research — interviews, contextual inquiry, usability testing, diary studies. Essential when you have 50+ observations and need to make sense of them before recommending anything.
methods.watch_out: Tempting to start with categories and sort into them. That's coding, not affinity diagramming. The whole point is bottom-up emergence. If you already know the categories, use thematic analysis instead.

methods.name: Thematic Analysis
methods.description: Systematic coding of qualitative data into themes. Unlike affinity diagramming (bottom-up, emergent), thematic analysis can be deductive (coding against a framework) or inductive (letting themes emerge). Six phases: familiarize, generate initial codes, search for themes, review themes, define and name themes, write up. The standard method for making qualitative research publishable.
methods.when: When you need rigorous, defensible qualitative findings — for academic publication, stakeholder reports, or cross-study comparison. Works on interview transcripts, open-ended survey responses, diary entries, think-aloud transcripts.
methods.watch_out: Inter-coder reliability matters if you want credibility. Two researchers should code a subset independently and compare before committing to the codebook. Solo thematic analysis is fast but hard to defend.

methods.name: Journey Mapping
methods.description: Visualize the end-to-end experience across time, touchpoints, channels, and emotional states. A journey map shows where friction accumulates, where handoffs break, and where the experience fails even though each individual screen works fine. The unit of analysis is the journey, not the page.
methods.when: When problems are cross-channel or cross-session — the user starts on mobile, continues on desktop, calls support, gets an email. Essential when individual usability tests show no issues but conversion or satisfaction is still poor.
methods.watch_out: A journey map without research data is fiction. Don't map what you think happens — map what you observed. Stakeholder assumptions are the starting point for research, not the map itself.

methods.name: Service Blueprint
methods.description: Extends the journey map below the line of visibility — what happens backstage to support what the user sees. Maps frontstage actions, backstage processes, support systems, and physical evidence in aligned swim lanes. Shows where internal failures cause external friction.
methods.when: When the user experience breaks because of operational, organizational, or technical failures invisible to the user. Common in e-commerce (fulfillment, returns), healthcare (referrals, records), and any service with human operators behind the interface.
methods.watch_out: Requires access to backstage operations — engineering, support, logistics. If you only have the user-facing side, you're building half a blueprint. The backstage is where the actionable fixes usually live.

methods.name: Competitive Analysis (UX)
methods.description: Systematic evaluation of competitor products against the same criteria you use for your own. Not feature comparison — UX evaluation: how do competitors handle the same user tasks, what patterns do they use, where do they fail, what can you learn without running your own study. Screenshot-driven, heuristic-scored, structured by task flow.
methods.when: Before major redesigns, when entering a new market, or when stakeholders ask 'what does everyone else do?' Structure it so the answer is evidence, not opinion.
methods.watch_out: Easy to turn into a feature matrix. Resist. The value is in evaluating execution quality, not counting features. A competitor can have the feature and still fail the interaction.

methods.name: Content Audit
methods.description: Inventory and evaluate all content in a system — pages, labels, help text, error messages, empty states, CTAs. Quantitative audit counts what exists; qualitative audit evaluates whether it works. Exposes redundancy, gaps, inconsistency, and content that actively harms the experience.
methods.when: Before any information architecture rework, migration, or redesign. When users report confusion but the interface 'looks fine' — the problem is often in the words, not the layout.
methods.watch_out: A spreadsheet of URLs is an inventory, not an audit. The evaluation — is this content accurate, useful, findable, consistent? — is where the value is. Budget time for the qualitative pass.

methods.name: Accessibility Audit
methods.description: Evaluate a product against WCAG 2.1 (or 2.2) success criteria at a target conformance level (A, AA, or AAA). Combines automated scanning (axe, Lighthouse) with manual testing — screen reader navigation, keyboard-only operation, color contrast, focus management, alternative text. Automated tools catch ~30% of issues; the rest require a human.
methods.when: Before launch, after major redesigns, or when legal compliance is required (EU European Accessibility Act 2025, ADA Section 508). Also valuable as a regular cadence — quarterly or per release.
methods.watch_out: Passing automated checks is not accessibility. Screen reader testing and keyboard navigation are where the real failures hide. Test with actual assistive technology, not just the audit tool.

methods.name: Stakeholder Interviews
methods.description: Structured interviews with internal stakeholders — product owners, engineers, support staff, executives — to understand business constraints, technical limitations, organizational politics, and unstated assumptions before starting user research. Not user research — context research.
methods.when: First week of any project. Before you talk to a single user, understand what the organization believes, what it fears, and what constraints are real versus assumed. Surfaces misalignment between teams early enough to address it.
methods.watch_out: Stakeholder beliefs about users are hypotheses, not data. Document them as assumptions to test, not as requirements to implement. The biggest risk is treating stakeholder interviews as a substitute for user research.

methods.name: Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA)
methods.description: Decompose a task into a hierarchy of goals, sub-goals, operations, and plans. Each goal breaks down until you reach operations a user can perform in one action. Plans describe the sequencing rules (do in order, select one, do simultaneously). The result is a tree that shows every path through a task and where complexity or error risk concentrates.
methods.when: When designing complex workflows, safety-critical systems, or multi-step processes. Before building, to understand the task structure. After building, to compare intended vs. actual task paths. Essential for automation design — you need to know the task structure before deciding what to automate.
methods.watch_out: Don't go deeper than you need. Three levels is usually enough for design decisions. Six levels of decomposition is a research project, not a design tool. Stop when the operations are actionable.
